scenario: AITA for refusing an additional guest at our wedding | Thanks for watching this post. First time writing here and non-native English speaker. I am getting married very soon. As you can imagine, this takes a lot of preparation. I'm talking here about the civil wedding, which will be very intimate and consequently restricted to our very close family: parents, siblings and, in my case, godparents and their children. The wedding will happen in another country, so this takes a lot of preparation as it is in another culture. When I made the invitations, I've been clear: I invited my parents (2 p.) and my godparents' family (4 p.). I've been very flexible, I told everyone that they could join us anytime they like (i.e., arrive in the country when they wish because I understand it's complicated when you have 4 different jobs etc) as long as they'll be present for the ceremony. Moreover, because the destination is far, my in-laws kindly proposed to offer the accommodation to all of them. The wedding is now in one month and I just received a message from my godmother saying that they have booked the flights, and they will be 5 because the gf of my cousin is joining. That's where I am really feeling uncomfortable: I receive this as a 'fait accompli' (done deal) without any prior consultation, without even asking me if that's ok to have an additional person (that I've never met). I've always been clear about the number of people invited. I just can't stand to receive this kind of 'news' via a late evening text message. It's not that I'm against that additional person. It's just the way that I'm put in front of this, as if I had nothing to say. And we're not talking about the 'party' wedding, but something very special that is meant to be in strict intimacy. Moreover, I know that they have their tickets since 1 month, and I was waiting for their news to plan the trip etc. So they literally waited 1 month to announce it, now that the date is getting closer. I just don't understand this kind of behavior. It costs nothing to make a quick phone call before booking anything, and to ask if it's possible, etc. In sum, they just invited someone at my wedding, someone that wasn't ever planned and that I don't even know. This morning, I sent a polite message saying: 'I'm confused by your news, I've always been clear about the number of guests and why I picked these specific guests (i.e. you) for our wedding. Why haven't you called me and asked me before booking anything? I'm put in front of a done deal, and I have to oppose myself to it, as it goes against the very idea of what we've been planning for months. The solution to this situation, I am afraid, does not lie within my hands. If X is feeling uncomfortable about this, I could understand, but with respect to my in-laws, I just cannot accept this compromise.' So: Am I the asshole? More precisely: Am I the asshole for refusing this, for writing to them clearly that it will not be possible and that they should have contacted me before doing anything? Thanks.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the person in this situation is "the asshole" for refusing an additional guest at their wedding. Let me break this down step by step. First, the person is getting married and has planned a very intimate civil ceremony. They've been clear about the guest list, inviting only close family and godparents. They've also mentioned that the wedding is in another country, which adds to the preparation and complexity. They've been flexible with the arrival times but have emphasized that everyone needs to be present for the ceremony. Now, the issue arises when the godmother informs them that they're bringing an additional person, the godfather of their cousin, making it five people instead of four. This was done without prior consultation, and the person feels uncomfortable because they were never asked if this was okay. They received this news via a text message, which they find disrespectful, especially since they've been clear about the guest numbers. The person sent a polite message expressing their confusion and discomfort, questioning why they weren't contacted before booking. They also mentioned that they can't accept this compromise, especially regarding their in-laws. So, the question is: Is the person the asshole for refusing this additional guest and for being clear about their boundaries? Let me consider the factors: 1. **Clarity on Guest List:** The person was explicit about the number of guests and who was invited. They've been consistent in their communication, which is important when planning such an intimate event. 2. **Communication Style:** The additional guest was added without prior discussion. The person received this information via text, which they found disrespectful, especially since they had been waiting for updates to plan accordingly. 3. **Impact on the Event:** The wedding is meant to be intimate. Adding an unexpected guest could disrupt the planned dynamics and make the event less special for the couple. 4. **Respect for Boundaries:** The person expressed that they feel their boundaries were crossed. It's reasonable to expect that any changes to the guest list would involve a discussion beforehand. 5. **Cultural and Logistics Considerations:** Since the wedding is in another country, logistics are more complex. The in-laws offered accommodation, which adds another layer of responsibility. Adding a guest without discussion could affect these arrangements. Now, considering whether the person is being unreasonable. They were clear about their expectations, communicated politely, and expressed their discomfort respectfully. They didn't refuse the guest out of meanness but because the way it was handled was disrespectful and went against their plans. On the other hand, the godmother's side didn't communicate beforehand, which could be seen as inconsiderate. They assumed the person would be okay with the additional guest without checking, which might be seen as presumptuous. In conclusion, the person is not being the asshole. They were clear, communicated their feelings respectfully, and had valid reasons for their discomfort. The issue lies more in the lack of communication from the godmother's side rather than the person's refusal.
